segments.title: Chương 165: 0165【Điều khoản Khoai tây】
segments.content:
Chapter 168: 0165 The Tudou Clause The negotiations began, starting with the business side of things.

Chen Guiliang asked, "What do you think is Tudou.com's core selling point?"

"UGC, user-generated and shared content," Wang Wei said with great confidence.

Chen Guiliang said, "That alone isn't enough. UGC can only retain creators and a small number of users. It can't retain the broader majority of ordinary users."

Wang Wei frowned and asked, "Why do you say that?"

"The biggest demand Chinese users have for video websites is to watch films, TV shows, and variety shows," Chen Guiliang said. "The works I'm referring to here are, one, domestic films, TV shows, and variety shows, and two, foreign films, TV shows, and variety shows with Chinese subtitles."

Wang Wei fell into silent thought, still not agreeing with this statement.

Chen Guiliang continued, "Videos shot by users themselves can only serve as a gimmick and an add-on to make Tudou.com famous quickly and attract users. To increase Tudou.com's traffic and retain users for the long term, you still need genuine films, TV shows, and variety shows."

"That requires purchasing copyrights," Wang Wei said.

Chen Guiliang said, "It would be best if we had money to purchase copyrights, of course, but you don't have any right now. Even with my investment, it won't be enough. We'll have to wait until after the next round of financing."

Wang Wei understood. "Are you suggesting we start with pirated content?"

Chen Guiliang corrected him, "Piracy sounds too harsh. Let's call it 'users' secondary creation'! Or, 'users' spontaneous re-uploading.' If any problems arise, it has nothing to do with the website. We just take the video down."

At this point, although Tudou.com and YouTube had preliminarily decided to focus on UGC, neither was doing it very thoroughly. It would be another few months before they both, almost simultaneously, underwent a major revamp, comprehensively imitating Flickr's sharing model.

Once Flickr's sharing model was out, both Tudou.com and YouTube's traffic exploded.

But the situations in China and the US were different, causing Tudou.com and YouTube to develop in different directions after 2007.

The core reason was what Chen Guiliang had just mentioned: Chinese users' demand for video websites was, for the time being, primarily focused on film and television entertainment—watching movies, TV series, animated shows, and variety programs!

User surveys at the time, with multiple choices allowed, showed watching movies at 77%, watching TV series at 70.5%, watching variety shows at 38.7%, and watching anime at 35%.

In contrast, only 14.6% liked to watch original videos, even less than the 29.2% who watched news and information.

When Chen Guiliang said this, Wang Wei was very unconvinced.

"How about this," Chen Guiliang said, "since you want to do UGC, do it more thoroughly. Imitate the Flickr model and carry out a full revamp. At the same time, create an account under the identity of a netizen and re-upload some films and TV shows. Use two or three months to compare which type of video gets the most views. I'm not talking about single video views, but the overall views for different categories."

Wang Wei was still considering it.

Chen Guiliang said, "Arguing is useless. Let's speak with facts."

"Alright," Wang Wei agreed.

Chen Guiliang said, "My suggestion is, in the early stages, rely on UGC to attract attention and on re-uploaded film and entertainment content to retain users. After the next round of financing, we can then start systematically purchasing copyrights. Of course, this is just a suggestion, for your reference only."

"If you accept my investment, I will help drive traffic to you from Xiaonei.com. We'll also launch an event encouraging Xiaonei.com students to film their own videos, post them on Tudou.com, and then embed their personal creative videos from Tudou.com onto their Xiaonei.com homepages. Xiaonei.com and Tudou.com can achieve a complementary synergy."

This last part made Wang Wei's heart leap.

He knew Xiaonei.com already had several million users. If Tudou.com could team up with Xiaonei.com, even if they only attracted one percent of those users, it would cause Tudou.com's traffic to surge.

What's more, he truly needed funding, and Chen Guiliang's willingness to invest couldn't be better.

But Chen Guiliang didn't talk about the investment. Instead, he started discussing the Flickr model.

"When I was building Tudou.com, I did indeed reference Flickr," Wang Wei admitted openly.

YouTube was actually the same; in the early days, they were all students of Flickr.

"But the imitation wasn't thorough enough," Chen Guiliang said.

Since last year, he had been frequently following American websites, and Flickr was one of the objects of his study.

Wang Wei's four partners all came over and sat down, listening to Chen Guiliang explain his specific views.

From how to encourage the UGC model, to re-uploading videos, to the grassroots parody culture, Chen Guiliang talked for over an hour.

They listened, stunned.

The finance and legal staff Chen Guiliang had brought along also sat listening on the side, feeling that their boss was incredibly awesome.

"It's getting late. I'll treat everyone to dinner," Chen Guiliang said, standing up.

"Okay."

Wang Wei led them to a restaurant outside the residential complex.

After ordering, Chen Guiliang continued, "Super Girl is incredibly popular right now, which is a perfect opportunity to run an event. Xiaonei.com will encourage users to upload videos of themselves singing to Tudou.com. We'll select a top ten, top seven, top three, and a champion based on the Tudou.com video views. Whether they imitate Super Girl or sing their own songs, it doesn't matter."

"To win a good ranking, they'll only have two choices. Either they are genuinely amazing singers and take a professional route, or they can only resort to parody, attracting attention through wacky antics."

"We can hold similar events from time to time. The potential of netizens is limitless. As long as we guide them to a good start, they will spontaneously create more interesting content."

"At the same time, re-upload domestic and foreign programs. Especially entertainment shows from Hong Kong, Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea, which can attract a lot of young people. Films and TV series should also be re-uploaded. Try your best to retain users."

"The internet speed is very slow right now. You'll have to figure out how to improve the user's viewing experience yourself."

"As long as you get the user numbers and traffic up, I can help you contact VCs next year. With funds from the next financing round, Tudou.com can slowly start buying copyrights for films and shows."

Wang Wei and his partners had always been in a hazy state about how to operate Tudou.com in the future. They knew they should do UGC, but that was it; they didn't know the specific operational details.

Now that Chen Guiliang had laid it all out, everyone had a sudden moment of clarity.

"It's late. We'll discuss the investment tomorrow," Chen Guiliang said before heading straight back to his hotel.

Wang Wei and his four partners returned to their three-bedroom apartment, unable to resist talking on the way back.

Su Bo, who was in charge of technology, remarked with emotion, "No wonder he can become a billionaire at 19. His vision is broad, his thinking is clear, and his ideas are so systematic."

Tao Pei, responsible for the webpage, customer service, and ad sales, said, "The more I think about it, the more feasible it seems. If we do as he says, we can definitely make Tudou.com big."

"I also think President Chen is right. If it were me, I'd definitely want to watch TV series and entertainment shows from Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Japan. The overall views for that content would probably be much higher than user-generated content."

Wang Wei didn't join the discussion, quietly listening to his partners' chatter.

The next day.

Chen Guiliang stated his investment proposal: "ByteDance will invest 1.6 million yuan for a 20% stake in Tudou.com. At the same time, ByteDance will drive traffic to Tudou.com for free and cooperate on the Super Girl parody show event. How about it?"

"Deal," Wang Wei agreed in one breath, without even trying to negotiate.

Tudou.com's financial situation was simple, hardly needing verification, and they weren't bothered with setting up an option pool yet.

After the investment, the equity structure was as follows: Wang Wei 76%, ByteDance 20%, and the other partners a total of 4%.

However, when Chen Guiliang took out the financing agreement, Wang Wei was a bit puzzled by the additional clauses.

Shi Qian, who had drafted the financing agreement for Chen Guiliang, was now gazing out the window with great interest, as if the world outside was magnificent.

Before joining ByteDance, Shi Qian had worked at King & Wood Mallesons for four years and had participated in or witnessed quite a few investment deals. But he had truly never encountered an additional clause like this one.

What clause?

The Tudou Clause!

In another timeline, just as Tudou.com was about to go public, Wang Wei's ex-wife showed up to divide their assets. The court directly froze his shares, causing Tudou.com's first IPO plan to fail.

From then on, the Tudou Clause was born in the Chinese investment circle.

Wang Wei himself even gave it that name.

At the time, William Zhu had posted on Weibo: "I've heard that many VCs/PEs are recently trying to add clauses to SA shareholder agreements, requiring the CEOs of their portfolio companies to get approval from the board, especially the preferred shareholders, before they can marry or divorce. If this is true, it is truly a tragedy."

Wang Wei commented under this post: "First there was the Sina structure, now there is the Tudou Clause. Let's all work hard and leave our mark on the history of corporate governance."

The additional clause Chen Guiliang provided, of course, didn't say that the CEO's marriage required the board's approval. That would violate the Marriage Law!

"Why is it that when I get married, I must sign a prenuptial agreement that clarifies the division of property in case of divorce?" Wang Wei was speechless as he looked at this clause.

Chen Guiliang asked, "Do you have a girlfriend?"

Wang Wei shook his head. "No."

Chen Guiliang said, "What if you have a girlfriend in the future, and you have a flash marriage and flash divorce before Tudou.com goes public, and she makes a fuss and applies to have your assets frozen?"

Wang Wei didn't know whether to laugh or cry. "I don't even have a girlfriend, where would a flash marriage and flash divorce come from?"

"In that case, you can just treat this clause as if it doesn't exist," Chen Guiliang said. "I'm just taking precautions, just in case."

"Fine, I'll sign." Wang Wei felt that Chen Guiliang was a lunatic.

The lunatic watched Wang Wei sign, his mood instantly brightening.

The landmine of a founder's divorce was finally eliminated.

Besides this clause, Chen Guiliang had added another one.

Namely, if Tudou.com undergoes a certain financing round, and the post-investment equity structure becomes too complex with the founder's stake being too low, ByteDance's investment can be preferentially withdrawn, with its shares acquired by the new investor.

This meant that if Tudou.com went through too many financing rounds, Chen Guiliang would just pull his investment and stop playing, making a tidy profit in the process.

With the time he would spend messing around with Tudou.com, he might as well go acquire AcFun and Bilibili.

But AcFun was also a bit of a mess, barely surviving after more than a decade. Its illegitimate son, Douyu Live, was at least worth a look, though.

Wang Wei held the freshly signed agreement, looking at that additional clause, and the more he looked, the more awkward he felt.

Damn it, I'm not even looking for a girlfriend.

What divorce?

(End of this chapter)
